result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**`git merge`** ties the two histories together with a new merge commit. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C  main
     \   \
      D---E---M  feature (after `git merge main`)
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes linear, as if you'd started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C  main
         \
          D'---E'  feature (after `git rebase main`)
```

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved as it happened, with branches | Rewritten, linear |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for replayed commits |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up or catch up with `main`.
- Merge when integrating into a shared branch, or when the branch has already been pushed and others may have based work on it.

Rebasing commits others already have forces them to reconcile diverged history, and pushing it requires a force-push (`--force-with-lease` is the safer form). That's the one real way to hurt yourself with rebase.
